chapters.name: Relations and Functions
tips: Check domain, codomain and range before deciding whether a function is one-one or onto.
Use the definition f(x1)=f(x2) => x1=x2 for one-one proofs.
For composition, verify that the output of the inner function lies in the domain of the outer function.
Do not assume an inverse exists; the function must be bijective for an inverse function.

chapters.name: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
tips: Write the principal-value range before simplifying an inverse-trigonometric expression.
Treat sin^-1 x, cos^-1 x and tan^-1 x as inverse functions, not reciprocals.
Check the sign and quadrant when using inverse-trigonometric identities.
Do not drop principal-value restrictions when converting between inverse functions.

chapters.name: Matrices
tips: Check matrix orders before addition or multiplication.
Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative: AB and BA must be treated separately.
For an inverse, first check that the matrix is square and nonsingular.
Keep row and column positions consistent when computing products and transposes.

chapters.name: Determinants
tips: Use the correct cofactor sign pattern when expanding a determinant.
Before using A^-1 = adj(A)/|A|, verify that |A| is non-zero.
For area questions, take the absolute value of the determinant expression.
When solving AX=B by inverse matrices, verify that the coefficient matrix is invertible.

chapters.name: Continuity and Differentiability
tips: Check continuity using limit equals function value at the point.
Choose the differentiation rule from the structure: product, quotient, chain or implicit differentiation.
For inverse-trigonometric derivatives, preserve the correct denominator and sign.
In parametric differentiation, divide dy/dt by dx/dt; do not differentiate as if y were directly a function of x.

Use sign changes of f' to establish increasing or decreasing intervals.
For maxima/minima, verify the required conditions rather than stopping at f'(x)=0.
In rate-of-change problems, define the variables and their relationship before differentiating.

chapters.name: Integrals
tips: Always include +C with an indefinite integral.
Look for substitution when the derivative of an inner expression is also present.
Use integration by parts when the integrand is a suitable product.
For definite integrals, apply limits after obtaining the antiderivative.
Use even/odd symmetry and definite-integral properties before doing long calculations.

tips: Sketch the curves or identify their intersection points before setting up an area integral.
Use upper minus lower when integrating with respect to x.
Split the interval when the upper/lower curve changes.
Use absolute area where the signed integral would otherwise cancel regions.

chapters.name: Differential Equations
tips: Identify whether the differential equation is separable, homogeneous or linear before starting.
For homogeneous equations, use y=vx and replace dy/dx accordingly.
For dy/dx + Py = Q, calculate the integrating factor before integrating.
Keep the arbitrary constant until the final step and apply any initial condition afterward.

chapters.name: Vector Algebra

Use the dot product for angles/projections and the cross product for perpendicular-area relationships.
Remember that l^2+m^2+n^2=1 for direction cosines.
Keep scalar and vector products distinct; their outputs are different types of quantities.

For skew-line distance, keep the vector order consistent in the scalar triple-product expression.
Check whether lines are parallel, intersecting or skew before choosing the distance method.

chapters.name: Probability
tips: Write the events clearly before applying conditional probability.
Check independence rather than assuming it from the wording.
Use total probability when the sample space is partitioned into mutually exclusive exhaustive cases.
For Bayes' theorem, identify the prior probabilities and the conditional probabilities before substituting.
